site.name: Chance Mine
site.location: Beaver Creek area southeast of Nederland / Boulder County Tungsten Mining District
overview: Chance Mine, historically called the Tungsten Mine, was an important early tungsten property southeast of Nederland in Boulder County's tungsten district.

U.S. Geological Survey records trace the mine from the first discovery of the vein in 1900 through intensive early production, renewed underground development during World War I, and later federal-supported work.

timeline.text: Prospector Henry Loughlin discovered the Tungsten vein but made no recorded shipments.
John McRay sank a 15-foot shaft and mined a small quantity of ore.
Orin Beach developed and patented claims on the Tungsten vein; subsequent company operations reportedly recovered about $175,000 in ore before the early workings were thought exhausted.
George Cowdery explored eastward on the 120-foot level and found a new ore shoot, leading to further underground development.
Federal exploration records and Colorado mine reports continued to list the Tungsten (Chance) Mine as a tungsten property operated by Tungsten Mining Company.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245 places the mine about 1 1/4 miles southeast of Nederland and about 3,300 feet west-southwest of Tungsten Mountain at roughly 8,530 feet elevation. The report describes the Tungsten and Chance names as referring to the same mine and documents its underground workings in detail.

The same federal history records early ore west of the shaft at very high reported tungsten grade and shows later development on deeper levels. A dedicated longitudinal projection of the Tungsten (Chance) workings was published from 1930 mine data.

A USGS/GNIS-derived mapped point for Tungsten Shaft at approximately 39.943598, -105.497775 is retained as a documented shaft-level component of the historic Tungsten/Chance mine. It is a historic mapped feature and does not imply that an open shaft or safe public access exists today.
